crit: Axial corallite at the tip of every branch, larger and often a different colour from the radial corallites along the sides.
Very variable forms: tables, plates, digitate, corymbose, arborescent thickets.
The most diverse shallow-water genus.
imr: Axial corallite at branch tips, different in size and form from the others.
Axial surrounded by radial corallites whose wall forms a cup.
Can also form plates and tables from clusters of branchlets.

Acropora.sum: Axial corallite at every branch tip, larger than the cup-like radial corallites around it.
info: The name comes from Greek akros (tip) and poros (pore): the pore at the branch tip, i.e. the axial corallite.

crit: Knobbly branches covered in skeletal bumps (verrucae).
Corallites immersed on and between the verrucae.
Fine fuzz of tentacles by day; some species form blades with meandering ends.
imr: Short, knobbly branches that may meander or form blades.
Branches covered in verrucae (purely ornamental), larger than a polyp.
Corallites immersed on the verrucae.

Pocillopora.sum: Branches covered in verrucae (bumps larger than a polyp), with corallites immersed on and between them.
info: Coral Finder (p. 6): corallites sit on and among the verrucae.

crit: Compact branches with blunt or slightly flattened ends, as if squeezed.
Tiny corallites (~1 mm) with skeletal hoods, giving a scaly look.
Coarser and rounder than Seriatopora.
imr: Blunt or slightly flattened branch tips, which may meander.
Hooded corallites (facing downwards).
Instructor's notes: From afar the skeleton looks smooth, unlike Pocillopora.

Stylophora.sum: Tiny hooded corallites (~1 mm) give a scaly look; blunt, slightly flattened branch tips.

crit: Thin, weakly tapered branches with rounded or clubbed ends.
No differentiated axial corallite (unlike Acropora).
Small corallites (1-2 mm), widely spaced and poorly developed; common in turbid water.
imr: No axial corallite.
Corallites look empty.
Smooth corallite surface.
Instructor's notes: Branch tips can fork.

Anacropora.sum: No axial corallite; small, widely spaced, empty-looking corallites on thin branches with rounded ends.

crit: Compact, tangled bushes of very fine branches with pointed or rounded tips.
Corallites (~1 mm) arranged in rows along the branches.
Finer than Stylophora and without hoods.
imr: Compact, tangled colonies of thin branches.
Black corallites arranged in rows.
No hooded corallites.
Seriatopora.mn: "Serius Black": serial black pores, in rows.

Seriatopora.sum: Corallites (~1 mm) in rows along very fine branches, no hoods; compact tangled bushes.

crit: Very small corallites (0.8-1.5 mm) with well-formed walls, giving a pitted surface.
Massive (large domes, micro-atolls), finger-like branches, or encrusting.
Corallites slightly larger and better defined than Montipora.
imr: Irregular branches or massive colonies.
Small corallites with well-formed walls.
Shared walls in a honeycomb pattern.

Tubular corallites with high thin walls, no costae or ornament.
Orange, yellow, pink; T. micranthus is dark green to black and tree-like (up to 1 m).
imr: Dark green to black.
No symbiotic algae: not a true reef builder.
A round, tubular corallite at the end of every branch; smooth coenosteum.

Rounded corallites (3-6 mm) with walls obscured by spines.
Rows of fine spines (costae) between corallites give a rough surface.
Looks like Acropora but has no axial corallite.
imr: Untidy branching tangles, sometimes from a basal plate.
Fine spines run between the large corallites.
Whole colony, corallites included, made of small beads.

Echinopora.sum: No axial corallite; rounded corallites (3-6 mm) with rows of fine spines between them, rough beaded surface.

crit: Massive, thick or encrusting.
Corallites (1.5-3 mm) lined with coarse, ragged spinules.
Irregular heights, corallites pointing in different directions; less neat than Cyphastrea.
imr: Massive.
Cylindrical corallites standing out from the surface.
Septa poorly developed, so corallites look like holes.

crit: Compact, spiky colonies.
Tubular corallites with protruding blade- or spine-like septa: distinctive.
Daytime tentacles may hide the septa.
imr: Spiky, star-like corallites with blade-like septa.
Tentacles sit outside the septa.

crit: Plates, vases, cups or crusts.
Corallites (2-5 mm) tubular or low and immersed, well spaced.
Surface between corallites always smooth, without ornament.
imr: Smooth coenosteum between corallites.
Thin plates, regular colony, flowery polyps.
Corallites 2-3 mm.

Corallites (6-8 mm) on one side only, inclined towards the colony margin (nose-like).
The look-alike Oxypora (family Lobophylliidae) has corallites that are not inclined.
imr: Large nose-shaped corallites facing out towards the colony edge.
Polyps have large mouths and no tentacles (they use slime).

Wide valleys (10-40 mm) with separate walls.
Large spiky septal teeth under fleshy, carpet-like tissue.
Now includes former Symphyllia (shared walls).
imr: Large, fleshy corallites that look isolated from each other.
Large, spiky septal teeth.
Separate or shared walls; shared walls often have a groove along the top.

Lobophyllia.sum: Large fleshy corallites or wide valleys (10-40 mm) with big spiky septal teeth under carpet-like tissue.
info: Symphyllia was merged into Lobophyllia in 2016 (Huang et al. 2016, Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society).

crit: Thick crusts, submassive, or bifacial leafy fronds.
Corallites without walls (2-4 mm) grouped in valleys separated by sharp-crested ridges.
Smooth septo-costae flow from one corallite to the next.
imr: Club-like or leafy colonies, with corallites on both sides.
Septo-costae flow between corallites: smooth, star-like look.
Corallites in parallel rows; ridges meander around several mouths.
Pavona.mn: A star in the pavement (Hollywood Walk of Fame).

Roughly parallel valleys (corallites without walls, 3-6 mm).
Septo-costae form fine regular ribs at right angles to the valleys, like a fingerprint.
imr: Valleys with parallel ridges.
Finely ribbed septa.
Leafy, laminar growth.

info: WoRMS places Pachyseris in its own family, Pachyseridae, since 2023 (Quek et al. 2023, Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution).

crit: Tangles of thin, fluted blades and upright spires.
Large corallites (1-1.5 cm), immersed, without walls, at the bottom of deep valleys.
Widely spaced septo-costae.
imr: Branches grow straight up from a common base.
Towering small plates of equal height.
Instructor's notes: Maze-like, with towering walls like hedges.

crit: Domes, mounds, thick plates: a brain coral.
Meandering valleys 4-10 mm wide, short to long.
Septa alternate, walls look ragged; NO paliform lobes.
imr: Classic brain coral; ridges short, medium, long or mixed.
Septa usually alternate in size or position.
Smooth valleys without paliform lobes.
Instructor's notes: Order of checks for meanders: paliform lobes present or absent first, then the neatness of Goniastrea, the zipper of Leptoria and the raggedness of Platygyra (Coral Finder p18).
Platygyra.mn: A plate in a gyre: gyre means disorder, ragged septa.

Platygyra.sum: Brain coral with ragged walls and alternating septa, NO paliform lobes; valleys 4-10 mm.
info: The name comes from Greek platys (flat) and gyros (circle).

crit: Massive, ridges or columns; brain coral with narrow valleys.
Septa equal in size and evenly spaced, like a zipper.
More regular and finer than Platygyra.
imr: Can be confused with Platygyra.
Larger colonies form ridges, columns, mounds.
Equal septa, zipper-like; valleys narrower than Platygyra.
Instructor's notes: Valleys so narrow that in photos you see only the ridges, not the valleys.

24 tentacles per polyp (12 in Alveopora).
Small-polyp forms are mistaken for Porites.
imr: Large, elongated polyps extended by day; retract if wafted.
24 tentacles; denser skeleton than Alveopora.
Instructor's notes: Tentacles typically pulse.

Stalks with costae visible under the vesicles.
Vesicles larger than in Euphyllia.
imr: Bubble coral: large grape-like vesicles.
Looks solitary, becomes a colony as an adult.

Coral Finder (p. 10) describes it as a stalked branching colony.

Plates, crusts, irregular branches; varied surface texture.
Corallites smaller and less distinct than Porites.
imr: Smallest corallites of all hard corals; can be confused with Porites.
Corallite walls poorly developed; corallites look empty.

Coenosteum covered in veins or conical mounds, in branching and massive forms.

Heavy, round skeleton with large septal teeth.
Looks like an anemone (or Catalaphyllia).
imr: Long, anemone-like tentacles out by day, white tips.

Size variable (4-20 mm); formerly Favia.

Colony does not look crowded.
Formerly Favia.

info: Indo-Pacific Favia species were moved to Dipsastraea in 2012 (Budd et al. 2012, Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society).

Extra-tentacular budding: small corallites appear between the large ones.
Strongly alternating septa; formerly Montastraea.
imr: Crowded colony of circular corallites.
Extra-tentacular budding (Dipsastraea: intra-tentacular).
Septa alternate in size; formerly Montastrea / Phymastrea.

Neat corallites and septa with a crown of paliform lobes always present.

Sub-angular, thin-walled corallites; septa often interlock.
Ridges wider at the base; walls often look bleached.

info: Corals of the World glossary: paliform lobes are upright skeletal lobes at the inner margin of the septa.

crit: Submassive or thick encrusting; corallites 3-8 mm, mostly with SHARED walls (cerioid).
Wall structure can be ambiguous: shared and separate walls in the same colony, with a shadow between sub-rounded corallites.
Extra-tentacular budding, like Astrea; more irregular than Goniastrea, paliform lobes uncommon.
imr: Often submassive or thick encrusting rather than massive.
Extra-tentacular budding, so can be confused with Astrea.
Separate-walled corallites often sub-rounded, with a shadow between them, on an uneven surface.
Wall structure can be ambiguous (shared and separate in one colony, e.g. F. rotundata); oral disc distinct from the shared wall.
Instructor's notes: Favites covers the extra-tentacular corals with shared or separate walls; Dipsastraea only the intra-tentacular, separate-walled ones (Favites still under review).

The branching D. axifuga (tubular corallites 10-14 mm, soft sediment) is the Coral Finder p9 form.
imr: Looks like Turbinaria, but corallites about 6 mm, thicker plates and a less regular colony.
The species here is D. peltata (formerly Turbinaria peltata, Coral Finder p50).

terms: Radial skeletal elements projecting inward from the corallite wall towards its centre; usually thin plates, in some genera only rows of spines.
Radial skeletal ribs outside the corallite wall, often continuing the septa.
Skeletal boundary around a corallite; separate or shared with neighbouring corallites.
Porous skeleton between corallites; in some taxa it also builds their walls.
The skeleton produced by one polyp.
Soft tissue around the mouth, inside the ring of tentacles.
Upright projections from the inner edges of the septa; may form a crown around the columella (central skeletal structure).
Opening at the centre of the oral disc, leading to the digestive cavity.
tips: Find the polyp mouth: is it raised or embedded?
Read the wall structure: shared, separate, or indistinguishable.
No visible walls? Look at the skeletal ornament: beads, spines, parallel striations.
Check the scale: corallites in mm or in cm?
